newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile plays down U.S. salmon dumping ruling.
newsitem.headline: Chile plays down U.S. salmon dumping ruling.

text.p: Chilean Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia played down Thursday a U.S. decision to continuing a probe into dumping claims against Chilean salmon farmers, saying the ruling was just the start of the investigation.
"This situation does not surprise us as it is only the beginning of the process," Garcia told a news conference.
"We were convinced that the investigation would go ahead. It does not surprise us that a ruling like this has happened.

The U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) ruled three to zero Thursday that there was evidence suggesting that Chilean salmon farmers received subsidies and were dumping fresh Atlantic salmon in the American market.
Garcia said the government would back any proposals by salmon producers to enter talks to resolve the dispute.
"We will support the private sector if the companies think it is possible to enter some form of negotiation," he said.
"It is not possible (to start talks) at this moment. This would be illegal under the United States anti-monopoly laws."
Earlier Thursday, Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza took a more aggressive stand against the ruling by the ITC
"I believe it is bad news in the sense that we don't believe there has been dumping, subsidies, damage or anything else," Insulza told reporters.
"We are unhappy with the ruling...we believe this problem should be stopped."
The Commerce Department, which is reponsible for the investigation, is expected to announce its decision on around September 5.
Chilean exports of trout and salmon to the United States soared from just $3.4 million in 1986 to $177 million last year.
American supermarkets and restaurants are Chile's largest market for fresh Atlantic salmon exports.
